facts.fact_text: The applicant planned a demonstration in order to draw attention to the plight of borrowers of foreign-currency loans.
On 8 October 2013 the applicant applied to the Budapest Police Department for acquiescence in a demonstration lasting from 17 October until 1 November 2013.
The demonstration applied for on 8 October 2013 was scheduled to be held in District II of Budapest, in the neighbourhood of the embassy of Israel.
The demonstration applied for on 8 October 2013 was also scheduled to be held in District XII of Budapest, in the neighbourhood of the permanent residence of the Prime Minister.
On 10 October 2013 the Budapest Police Department dismissed the applicant's application for acquiescence in the demonstration.
The applicant sought judicial review of the Budapest Police Department's decision of 10 October 2013.

Section 8(1) of the Assembly Act (Act no. III of 1989) provides that if the holding of an event subject to prior notification seriously endangers the proper functioning of the representative bodies or courts, or the circulation of traffic cannot be secured by another route, the police may ban the holding of the event at the place or time indicated in the notification, within forty-eight hours of receipt of the notification by the authority.
Section 8(2) of the Assembly Act (Act no. III of 1989) provides that the decision of the police shall be communicated to the organiser in writing within 24 hours.
The Budapest Police Department observed that on 2 October 2013, closure of the District XII venue had been ordered by the Counter-Terrorism Centre.
The closure measure of the District XII venue was in place from 3 October until 31 December 2013.
The Budapest Police Department observed that on 2 October 2013, closure of the District XII venue had been ordered by the Counter-Terrorism Centre.
The closure of the District XII venue was ordered by the Counter-Terrorism Centre in view of the impending visit of the ambassador of Israel and other protected persons.

The Budapest Administrative and Labour Court observed that there were a number of competing rights at stake: the applicant's right to freedom of assembly, on the one hand; and the rights of others to respect for their private life and free movement, and an official dignitary's right to statutory protection, on the other.

In the Budapest Administrative and Labour Court's view, the rights of others to respect for their private life and free movement, and an official dignitary's right to statutory protection, outweighed the applicant's interest in having the demonstration at the desired locations.

In the Budapest Administrative and Labour Court's view, the rights of others to respect for their private life and free movement, and an official dignitary's right to statutory protection, outweighed the applicant's interest in having the demonstration at the desired locations.

The Constitutional Court observed that the Budapest Administrative and Labour Court had construed the rights to respect for private life and free movement, as well as an official dignitary's right to statutory protection, as grounds for restricting the right to freedom of assembly.

The Constitutional Court found that the Budapest Administrative and Labour Court's reasoning amounted to an unlawful broadening of the scope of exhaustive reasons for the prohibition of a demonstration as contemplated in section 8(1) of the Assembly Act (Act no. III of 1989).
